parties.petitioner: The Chief Manager, Central Bank of India & Ors.
parties.respondent: M/s Ad Bureau Advertising Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.

summary: The main issue was whether a borrower of a project loan qualifies as a 'consumer' under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986. The National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC) held that the bank was deficient in service for wrongly reporting the respondent as a defaulter to CIBIL despite accepting a one-time settlement and issuing a no-dues certificate, causing reputational and financial harm, including loss of an advertising tender. The NCDRC awarded ₹75 lakhs in compensation and directed the bank to issue a clarification certificate. The Supreme Court considered arguments on the definition of 'consumer', particularly whether the loan was for commercial purposes, and examined precedent on business-to-business transactions and dominant intention of profit generation.
legal_provisions_cited: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002
Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993, Section 19(1)
National Insurance Company Limited vs. Harsolia Motors & Ors. (2023) 8 SCC 362
Lilavati Kirtilal Mehta Medical Trust vs. Unique Shanti Developers (2020) 2 SCC 265
final_judgment: Pending final determination of the appeals, the Supreme Court upheld the NCDRC's finding of deficiency in service due to incorrect reporting of the respondent as a defaulter, affirming the compensation and directions for corrective action by the bank, subject to the ongoing legal examination of consumer status under the Act.
